opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What I value most about the research behind the MuVR series is less any single result and more the way of working that produced it.

The first thing is honesty about what actually matters. In this field it's easy to chase leaderboard numbers or a flashy demo. The work I'm proudest of started from a plain question: what capability is really missing, and what would it take to build it properly? Sometimes that meant spending a long time on unglamorous things like data quality, evaluation design, and training stability before anything exciting happened.

The second thing is the team. Good research here is rarely one person's idea. It comes from a small group who trust each other enough to argue hard, kill their own ideas quickly when the experiments say no, and keep going when the path isn't clear. I've learned that the culture of a team, how it handles failure and whether people feel free to try strange things, shapes the results more than people outside realize.

The third is treating each version as a step, not an endpoint. Every release taught us something we didn't know: where the model was brittle, where our assumptions were wrong, what users actually needed. I value that iterative humility. You build, you look carefully at what broke, and you let that change your thinking for the next round.

And finally, I care that the work is useful beyond us. If other researchers can build on it, reproduce it, or even prove us wrong, that's when research really has value. So for me, the MuVR work is a way of getting a little closer to the capabilities we believe matter, and doing it in a way that pushes the whole field forward, not just our own numbers.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. What I value most about the MuVR work is honestly less any single result and more the way the team chose to work.

When we started, the obvious path would have been to take whatever was working elsewhere, scale it up, and report numbers. We deliberately didn't do that. We spent a long time at the beginning just asking what the real bottleneck was, and we kept coming back to the same answer: the models weren't failing because they lacked capacity, they were failing because the training signal was wrong. So a lot of the early effort went into things that don't look impressive on a leaderboard, like how we construct data, how we verify it, and how we decide what counts as a good trajectory before we ever run a large job.

The second thing I value is that we treated efficiency as a first-class research question, not an engineering afterthought. There's a tendency in this field to assume that if you have enough compute, the method doesn't matter. We didn't have that luxury, and I think that constraint made the research better. Every design choice had to justify itself. If a component didn't move the needle, it came out, and that discipline carried through the whole series.

And then there's the people side. The MuVR team was very young, mostly researchers who hadn't been through a big release before. We gave them real ownership. Someone would be responsible for a whole piece end to end, from the idea to the ablations to writing it up. That's uncomfortable at first, people make mistakes, but it's also how you build researchers who can actually think rather than just execute. Looking back, I'm probably proudest of that. The models will be replaced eventually. The habits and the taste those people developed will outlast any particular checkpoint.
